title: pow_2ToUInt reverts on NaN and Infinity inputs instead of returning sentinel values
description: In pow_2ToUInt, when the input x is NaN (xExponent == 0x7FFF && xSignifier != 0), the function calls toUInt(NaN). The NaN constant has exponent 0x7FFF = 32767, which exceeds the overflow threshold of 16638 checked inside toUInt via require(exponent <= 16_638). This causes an unconditional revert. Similarly, toUInt(POSITIVE_INFINITY) also has exponent 0x7FFF and will revert. The same pattern applies to the xExponent > 16_397 branch where xNegative is false: toUInt(POSITIVE_INFINITY) is called and reverts. These are supposed to be error-handling paths but instead cause unhandled reverts.
message: Any smart contract integrating pow_2ToUInt that can receive NaN or out-of-range quadruple precision inputs will experience a revert at these code paths. If the calling contract does not handle reverts from this library (e.g., it uses the result in a critical path), it will be permanently broken/DoS'd for those inputs. Protocols relying on this for financial calculations (e.g., interest rate models, AMM pricing) could be griefed by supplying inputs that trigger the NaN/Infinity paths.
recommendation: Replace the calls to toUInt() with direct return values for special cases. For NaN and overflow, return 0 or type(uint256).max as appropriate sentinels, rather than delegating to toUInt() which is not designed to handle infinities/NaN: if (xExponent == 0x7FFF && xSignifier != 0) { return 0; } // NaN ... if (!xNegative) { return type(uint256).max; } // +Infinity else { return 0; } // -Infinity mapped to zero
exploit_scenario: 1. Call pow_2ToUInt with x = NaN (0x7FFF8000000000000000000000000000). 2. xExponent = 0x7FFF, xSignifier = 0x8000000000000000000000000000 != 0. 3. The first branch fires: return toUInt(NaN). 4. Inside toUInt, exponent = uint128(NaN) >> 112 & 0x7FFF = 0x7FFF = 32767. 5. require(32767 <= 16638) fails → revert. Expected: return 0 or max uint as sentinel. Actual: revert.

title: Check-Effects-Interactions Violation in removeLiquidityImbalanced
description: In `removeLiquidityImbalanced`, tokens are transferred to `recipient` BEFORE the LP token burn occurs. The sequence is: (1) transfer tokens out, (2) calculate lpAmountIn, (3) burn LP from msg.sender. This violates the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. If any of the tokens in the Well are ERC777 tokens (with `tokensReceived` hooks) or any other token with transfer callbacks, the recipient contract's callback executes AFTER tokens are received but BEFORE the LP is burned. Although the `nonReentrant` modifier prevents direct reentrancy into Well state-changing functions, the callback can interact with OTHER contracts or manipulate state in ways that affect the subsequent LP burn calculation. Furthermore, `msg.sender` (the LP burner) and `recipient` (token receiver) can be different addresses, meaning the LP burn validation happens against msg.sender's balance while tokens were already sent to recipient.
message: With callback tokens (ERC777), an attacker acting as recipient can observe the token receipt and take actions in other protocols using the received tokens before the LP is burned. More critically, if the well function's calcLpTokenSupply result can be influenced by external state during the callback window, the lpAmountIn calculation could be manipulated to burn fewer LP tokens than the tokens received are worth, extracting value from the pool.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy malicious contract that implements ERC777 tokensReceived hook. 2. Call removeLiquidityImbalanced with large tokenAmountsOut, recipient = malicious contract. 3. Tokens transfer to malicious contract, triggering tokensReceived callback. 4. In callback, attacker uses received tokens in external DeFi protocols before their LP is burned. 5. Back in removeLiquidityImbalanced, lpAmountIn is calculated and burned from msg.sender. 6. Net effect: attacker had use of tokens before paying LP cost, enabling flash-loan-like arbitrage within the callback window.

title: uint128 Reserve Overflow Causes Silent State Corruption
description: Reserves are stored as packed uint128 values via `LibBytes.storeUint128`. However, there is no validation anywhere in the code that reserves fit within uint128 bounds (max ~3.4 × 10^38). All arithmetic on reserves uses uint256. If a token has 18 decimals and high liquidity, reserves could exceed uint128 max. When `LibBytes.storeUint128` is called with a value exceeding uint128 max, the upper bits are silently truncated, corrupting the stored reserve value. On the next call, `_getReserves` returns the truncated value, making the Well believe it holds far fewer tokens than it actually does.
message: If reserves overflow uint128: (1) Stored reserves become drastically smaller than actual balances. (2) Subsequent swaps and liquidity operations compute incorrect amounts. (3) LP holders could drain more tokens than they are entitled to by exploiting the discrepancy between actual balances and stored reserves. (4) The protocol becomes permanently insolvent for that pool.
exploit_scenario: 1. Find or create a Well with a high-decimal token (e.g., 18 decimals). 2. Add liquidity until reserves[i] > type(uint128).max (~3.4e38 tokens, ~3.4e20 in 18-decimal units). 3. _setReserves calls LibBytes.storeUint128 which truncates to uint128. 4. _getReserves now returns corrupted low value. 5. calcLpTokenSupply with wrong reserves mints wrong LP amounts. 6. Attacker exploits discrepancy to withdraw more tokens than deposited.

title: First Liquidity Provider LP Token Inflation Attack
description: When the Well has zero liquidity (totalSupply == 0), the first LP provider can manipulate the initial LP token price. The `_addLiquidity` function calls `_calcLpTokenSupply(wellFunction(), reserves) - totalSupply()`. With totalSupply == 0, lpAmountOut equals the raw output of the well function. An attacker can: (1) Be the first depositor with minimal amounts to get a small LP amount, (2) Directly transfer large amounts of tokens to the Well contract, (3) Call `sync()` to mint LP tokens based on the inflated balances. This inflates the LP token price, causing subsequent depositors to receive zero or near-zero LP tokens due to rounding in the well function, while the attacker's LP tokens are worth far more than deposited.
message: Attacker can steal funds from subsequent liquidity providers. If the well function rounds down LP token output for subsequent depositors, those depositors receive fewer LP tokens than their pro-rata share, effectively donating funds to the first depositor/attacker.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker calls addLiquidity with minimal amounts (1 wei each token), receives small LP amount. 2. Attacker directly transfers large amounts of both tokens to the Well contract (bypassing reserves). 3. Attacker calls sync() to receive LP tokens for the excess balance. 4. Well function now has high reserve-to-LP-supply ratio. 5. Victim calls addLiquidity with proportional amounts. 6. Due to rounding in calcLpTokenSupply, victim receives 0 LP tokens but tokens are accepted. 7. Attacker calls removeLiquidity to extract victim's tokens.

title: Malicious Well Function Can Drain Pool Funds
description: The Well contract makes unchecked external calls to `wellFunctionAddress()` for all critical calculations: `calcLpTokenSupply`, `calcReserve`, and `calcLPTokenUnderlying`. These calls are made via `IWellFunction(_wellFunction.target).calcReserve(...)`. If the well function address is set to a malicious contract (possible if the Aquifer deployer is compromised or the system allows user-specified well functions), the malicious contract can return arbitrary values for reserves and LP token supply calculations. Additionally, even a legitimate well function with a bug can return incorrect values that allow value extraction.
message: A malicious well function can: (1) Return inflated amountOut for swaps, draining the pool. (2) Return deflated lpAmountIn for removeLiquidityImbalanced, allowing free token withdrawals. (3) Return zero for calcLpTokenSupply to allow minting unlimited LP tokens. The entire TVL of the Well can be drained in a single transaction.
recommendation: Add sanity checks on well function outputs: (1) Verify calcReserve output is within reasonable bounds relative to input reserves. (2) Verify calcLpTokenSupply is monotonically related to reserves. (3) Consider adding a whitelist of approved well functions at the Aquifer level with formal verification. (4) At minimum, add bounds checks: `require(reserve > 0 && reserve <= currentReserve * MAX_RESERVE_RATIO)`.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy malicious WellFunction contract where calcReserve always returns 0 for token j. 2. Create Well with malicious well function via Aquifer. 3. Call swapFrom: reserves[j] = calcReserve() = 0, so amountOut = reserveJBefore - 0 = entire reserve. 4. Entire balance of token j is transferred to attacker. Note: This depends on Aquifer access controls, but the Well itself has no validation of well function behavior.

title: Pump Update with Stale Reserves Enables Oracle Manipulation
description: In `_updatePumps`, the stored reserves (not actual token balances) are passed to pump updates. The reserves are read via `_getReserves()` which reads from packed storage. If any operation leaves reserves in an inconsistent state (e.g., if `_setReserves` is never called due to a revert after pump update), the pump receives stale data. More critically, in the `shift()` function flow: `_updatePumps` is called with stored reserves, then actual balances are read. The pump has already been updated with old reserves before the shift is processed. This means the pump (oracle) records the pre-shift state, missing the price impact of the shift operation. An attacker can exploit this by: (1) Manipulating balances via direct transfers, (2) Calling shift to update reserves without updating the pump with correct post-shift reserves.
message: Pump-based oracles (e.g., Beanstalk's price oracle) receive incorrect price data. This can lead to protocol-level exploits in systems relying on Well price oracles for collateral valuation, liquidations, or minting decisions. An attacker can manipulate the oracle reading while keeping the Well's internal state consistent.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker directly transfers large amount of tokenA to Well (no pump update). 2. Attacker calls shift(tokenB, 0, attacker): _updatePumps called with old (pre-transfer) reserves - pump records old price. 3. shift calculates amountOut using actual balances (including donated tokenA), gets large tokenB output. 4. tokenB transferred to attacker, reserves updated with new state. 5. Pump has recorded old price despite large price movement - oracle is stale/manipulated. 6. Attacker uses manipulated pump oracle in dependent protocol for profit.

title: calcReservesAtRatioSwap Return Value Ignored - Rate Cap Silently Fails
description: In `_capRates`, when the rate exceeds the limit (either upward or downward), `calcReservesAtRatioSwap` is called but its return value is completely ignored. The function modifies `reserves` internally (it does mutate the array in-place via `reserves[i]` and `reserves[j]` assignments), but examining `calcReservesAtRatioSwap`: it assigns `reserves[j]` and `reserves[i]` directly on the passed array. However, `cappedReserves` is passed as memory array - Solidity passes memory arrays by reference, so mutations DO propagate back. BUT the return value `reserves` is not reassigned. Let me re-examine: `calcReservesAtRatioSwap` takes `uint256[] memory reserves` and does `reserves[j] = ...` and `reserves[i] = cappedReserveI` - since memory arrays are passed by reference in internal calls but this is a `private view` call... Actually the mutations DO happen in-place since it's the same memory pointer. However this needs deeper verification. The critical issue is that `_capRates` returns `cappedReserves = reserves` at the start, then modifies `reserves` in-place via `calcReservesAtRatioSwap`. Since `cappedReserves` and `reserves` point to the same array, mutations propagate. BUT: `tryCalcReserveAtRatioSwap` uses `try wf.calcReserveAtRatioSwap(reserves, i, ratios, data)` - this is an external call, so a copy of `reserves` is sent. The returned value updates `reserves[i]` and `reserves[j]` in the local copy. This means the rate-capping logic DOES work correctly via in-place mutation of the memory array. Re-examining more carefully: the real issue is that `calcReservesAtRatioSwap` is `private view` and it calls `tryCalcReserveAtRatioSwap` which is an external call. External calls encode arguments as calldata (copying), so the external well function receives a copy. The local `reserves` array IS mutated by `reserves[j] = ...` and `reserves[i] = cappedReserveI`. Since `cappedReserves` in `_capRates` IS the same memory pointer as `reserves` passed to `calcReservesAtRatioSwap`, mutations propagate back to `cappedReserves`. So rate capping DOES work. The actual critical issue here is that the return statement `return reserves` in `calcReservesAtRatioSwap` is not used by the caller, but since mutation is in-place, this is okay. Let me focus on the real vulnerabilities.
message: Rate capping appears to function due to in-place array mutation, so this specific concern is lower severity. Re-evaluating.
recommendation: For clarity and safety, explicitly assign the return value: `cappedReserves = calcReservesAtRatioSwap(...)`
exploit_scenario: N/A - in-place mutation makes this work

title: Division by Zero in calcCapExponent When capInterval is Zero
description: The `calcCapExponent` function computes `((deltaTimestamp - 1) / capInterval + 1)`. If `capInterval` is zero (either by misconfiguration or malicious data construction), this causes a division-by-zero panic, reverting the transaction. Since `capInterval` is decoded directly from the `data` parameter in `update()`, `readCappedReserves()`, `readInstantaneousReserves()`, and `_readCumulativeReserves()`, any caller passing `capInterval = 0` will cause a revert. For `update()`, this means the pump can be permanently bricked for a well if the well is initialized with `capInterval = 0` in its pump data, since every subsequent `update()` call will revert after initialization.
message: Permanent DoS of the pump for any well that uses capInterval=0 in its configuration. All update calls will revert, making the oracle permanently stale after the first update.
recommendation: Add a validation check: `require(capInterval > 0, 'capInterval must be positive');` at the start of `update()` and other functions that call `calcCapExponent`.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy a Well with MultiFlowPump configured with capInterval=0 in the pump data. 2. Call update() once to initialize (returns early). 3. Call update() again after time passes - calcCapExponent is called with capInterval=0, causing division by zero revert. 4. Pump is permanently stuck and cannot update.

title: Missing Overflow Check in _capLpTokenSupply Decrease Branch
description: In the LP token supply decrease branch of `_capLpTokenSupply`, the code computes: `uint256 minLpTokenSupply = lastLpTokenSupply * (ABDKMathQuad.ONE.sub(crp.maxLpSupplyDecrease)).powu(capExponent).to128x128().toUint256() / CAP_PRECISION2;`. Unlike the increase branch which checks `if (tempExp.cmp(MAX_CONVERT_TO_128x128) != -1)` before calling `.to128x128()`, the decrease branch has NO such overflow check. If `(ONE.sub(crp.maxLpSupplyDecrease)).powu(capExponent)` overflows the 128x128 fixed-point representation (i.e., the result is >= MAX_CONVERT_TO_128x128), then `.to128x128()` will produce an incorrect result or panic. This can happen with adversarial `maxLpSupplyDecrease` values close to 0 (meaning near-zero decrease allowed) combined with large `capExponent` values.
message: Incorrect cap calculation for LP token supply decreases, potentially allowing larger reserve changes than intended, undermining the MEV resistance of the oracle. Could also cause unexpected reverts.
recommendation: Add the same overflow check as in the increase branch: `bytes16 tempExp = (ABDKMathQuad.ONE.sub(crp.maxLpSupplyDecrease)).powu(capExponent); uint256 minLpTokenSupply; if (tempExp.cmp(MAX_CONVERT_TO_128x128) != -1) { minLpTokenSupply = 0; } else { minLpTokenSupply = lastLpTokenSupply.mulDiv(tempExp.to128x128().toUint256(), CAP_PRECISION2); }`
exploit_scenario: 1. Configure a well with maxLpSupplyDecrease very close to 0 (e.g., 0.001%). 2. Allow many blocks to pass (large deltaTimestamp, thus large capExponent). 3. Call update() or readCappedReserves(). 4. The powu() result for (1 - ~0).pow(largeN) approaches 1 with large exponent which would not overflow, but with invalid maxLpSupplyDecrease values > 1 (malformed bytes16), overflow is possible. 5. The to128x128() call produces incorrect results without the overflow guard.

title: Unsafe uint256-to-uint40 Truncation of startTimestamp in readTwaReserves
description: In `readTwaReserves`, the `startTimestamp` parameter is declared as `uint256` but silently truncated to `uint40` via `uint40(startTimestamp)`. The comment even acknowledges this: 'Overflow is desired on startTimestamp, so SafeCast is not used.' However, this means that if a caller passes a `startTimestamp` value greater than `type(uint40).max` (approximately year 36812), the truncation silently produces a completely different timestamp. More practically, if a legitimate startTimestamp (e.g., current Unix timestamp ~1.7 billion, fits in uint40) is passed with any high bits set due to encoding issues, it could compute a wrong deltaTimestamp. The 'overflow is desired' comment seems to refer to the subtraction `uint40(block.timestamp) - lastTimestamp` wrapping correctly, but the outer cast `uint40(startTimestamp)` could produce an incorrect startTimestamp if the caller passes a value > uint40 max by mistake, silently computing wrong TWA reserves instead of reverting.
message: TWA (time-weighted average) reserves computed over an incorrect time window, producing wrong price oracle values. Protocols relying on readTwaReserves for pricing could use incorrect prices, potentially enabling arbitrage or economic exploits.
recommendation: Validate that startTimestamp fits within uint40 range, or use SafeCast.toUint40(): `uint40 startTs = SafeCast.toUint40(startTimestamp);` This will revert if the value doesn't fit, preventing silent incorrect calculations.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker calls readTwaReserves with startTimestamp = 2^40 + validTimestamp. 2. uint40 truncation strips the high bit, yielding validTimestamp as the start. 3. deltaTimestamp is computed as if starting from validTimestamp. 4. The TWA reserve calculation uses this corrupted window, returning incorrect prices. 5. Any protocol using this for price determination is affected.

title: Arbitrary Caller Can Update Pump State for Any Address via msg.sender Slot
description: The `update()` function is callable by any address (no access control). It uses `msg.sender` as the well address to derive the storage slot: `slot = _getSlotForAddress(msg.sender)`. This means any attacker can call `update()` directly (not from a Well contract) and write to the storage slot corresponding to their own address. While this only corrupts the pump state for `msg.sender` as a 'well', there is a more serious issue: an attacker could deploy a contract at a specific address (using CREATE2) that corresponds to a legitimate well's storage slot. More practically, an attacker who IS a well operator or controls msg.sender can pass arbitrary `reserves` and `data` to manipulate the oracle state for their address. The pump trusts that only legitimate Wells call `update()`, but there is no verification that `msg.sender` is a legitimate Well. An EOA or malicious contract can call `update()` with crafted reserves to set arbitrary oracle values for their address, which other contracts might then query via `readInstantaneousReserves(attackerAddress, data)`.
message: Any contract or EOA can initialize and manipulate oracle state for any address they control as msg.sender. If another protocol queries the pump for an address controlled by the attacker, it receives manipulated oracle data. This enables price oracle manipulation for any well address the attacker controls.
recommendation: Add validation that msg.sender is a legitimate Well by checking it implements the IWell interface, or maintain a registry of authorized wells. At minimum, verify that IWell(msg.sender).getReserves() matches the passed reserves.
exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker deploys a malicious contract at address X. 2. Attacker calls multiFlowPump.update([1, 1000000000], data) from address X, initializing the oracle for address X. 3. After one block, calls update([1, 1], data) to manipulate the price down. 4. Any protocol that queries readInstantaneousReserves(X, data) receives manipulated data. 5. If the protocol was configured to use X as a well address, it receives the manipulated price.

title: Unvalidated External Call Data Parameters Enable Malicious Well Function Manipulation
description: In `_capReserves`, the function calls `IWell(well).wellFunction()` to get the well function address (`wf.target`). This well function address is then used to call `calcRate()`, `calcLpTokenSupply()`, `calcReserveAtRatioSwap()`, and `calcLPTokenUnderlying()`. In the context of `update()`, `well = msg.sender`, so the pump calls back into the calling contract (`msg.sender.wellFunction()`). A malicious caller can implement `wellFunction()` to return an arbitrary address as `wf.target`, causing the pump to call into any arbitrary contract. While these are `view` calls (no state modification intended), the `try/catch` wrappers mean failures are silently swallowed. A malicious well function could: (1) return crafted reserve values that bypass caps, (2) cause the cap calculations to silently fail and return max values, effectively disabling the MEV protection entirely.
message: A malicious Well can completely bypass the rate and LP supply caps by returning a crafted well function that always returns favorable values to `calcRate` and `calcLpTokenSupply`. This undermines the entire MEV resistance mechanism of the pump, allowing price manipulation within a single block.
recommendation: The pump should not trust the well's self-reported well function for cap calculations. Consider storing the well function address at initialization time, or using a registry of approved well functions. Alternatively, validate that the well function address is on an allowlist.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy MaliciousWell that implements IWell but returns a malicious IMultiFlowPumpWellFunction. 2. Malicious well function's calcRate() always returns lastRate (no cap triggered). 3. Malicious well function's calcLpTokenSupply() always returns lastSupply (no cap triggered). 4. MaliciousWell calls pump.update() with heavily manipulated reserves. 5. All cap checks pass because the well function reports no changes. 6. The pump stores the manipulated reserves as legitimate capped values. 7. Other protocols reading from this pump address receive manipulated oracle data.

title: Copy-Paste Bug in decodeWellData: decimal1 Never Set to Default 18
description: In `decodeWellData`, the default value check for `decimal1` is incorrectly written as `if (decimal0 == 0)` instead of `if (decimal1 == 0)`. This means if `decimal1` is passed as 0, it remains 0 instead of being defaulted to 18. A `decimal1` value of 0 causes `10 ** (18 - 0) = 10**18` scaling, leading to massively inflated reserve scaling in `getScaledReserves`, which completely breaks all pricing calculations.
message: If `decimal1` is 0 (e.g., passed intentionally or by mistake), reserves for token 1 are scaled by 10^18 instead of 1, causing completely wrong LP token supply calculations, incorrect swap amounts, and potentially allowing an attacker to drain reserves by exploiting the mispriced AMM.
exploit_scenario: 1. Deploy well with decimal1=0 (or rely on default path). 2. Call calcLpTokenSupply or any pricing function. 3. scaledReserves[1] = reserves[1] * 10^18 instead of reserves[1]. 4. All downstream calculations (lpTokenSupply, swap amounts) are wildly incorrect. 5. Attacker can exploit mispriced swaps to extract value.

title: calcReserveAtRatioSwap and calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity Return 0 on Non-Convergence
description: Unlike `calcReserve` which reverts with 'did not find convergence', both `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` silently return 0 (the default uint256 value) if the 255-iteration loop completes without convergence. A return value of 0 for a reserve is semantically invalid and would cause callers to operate on completely wrong state.
message: If convergence fails, callers receive reserve=0, which could cause downstream contracts to miscalculate swap amounts, allow zero-cost trades, or trigger other invariant violations. Protocols relying on these functions for price checks would receive invalid data silently.
recommendation:
Add a revert after each loop, similar to calcReserve:

revert("calcReserveAtRatioSwap: did not find convergence");
exploit_scenario: 1. Construct edge-case inputs (e.g., extreme price ratios far outside LUT range) that prevent convergence within 255 iterations. 2. Call calcReserveAtRatioSwap or calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity. 3. Function returns 0. 4. Caller uses 0 as a reserve value, breaking AMM invariants.

title: Division by Zero in getBandC When reserves Parameter is Zero
description: In `getBandC`, the calculation `c = lpTokenSupply * lpTokenSupply / (reserves * N) * ...` will revert with division by zero if `reserves == 0`. This is called from `calcReserve` with the other token's reserve. If one reserve is 0 (e.g., during initial pool setup or after a complete drain), the function panics. The comment in `calcLpTokenSupply` acknowledges division by zero may occur but says 'only withdrawal will work', however in `calcReserve` there's no such protection.
message: If either reserve is 0, `calcReserve` reverts, making it impossible to perform swaps or calculate LP tokens in edge cases. This could brick the pool temporarily or permanently depending on state.
recommendation: Add a zero-check guard: `if (reserves == 0) revert InvalidReserves();` in `getBandC` or handle the edge case in `calcReserve`.
exploit_scenario: 1. Pool has token0 reserve = X, token1 reserve = 0. 2. Call calcReserve(reserves, 0, lpTokenSupply, data). 3. getBandC is called with reserves = scaledReserves[1] = 0. 4. Division by zero revert.

title: updateReserve Can Underflow/Revert When Step Size Exceeds Current Reserve
description: In `updateReserve`, when `pd.targetPrice > pd.currentPrice`, the function subtracts from `reserve`: `reserve - pd.maxStepSize * (pd.targetPrice - pd.currentPrice) / (pd.lutData.highPrice - pd.lutData.lowPrice)`. If the computed step size exceeds `reserve`, this underflows and reverts in Solidity 0.8.x. This can happen when the price difference is large relative to the LUT range. The loop in `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` would then revert entirely rather than converging.
message: Denial of service for `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` when price targets require large reserve adjustments, preventing the protocol from correctly pricing swaps or liquidity operations.
exploit_scenario: 1. Call calcReserveAtRatioSwap with extreme targetPrice near edge of LUT range. 2. updateReserve computes step > current reserve. 3. Subtraction underflows, revert. 4. Function cannot converge, returns 0 or reverts.

title: Trusted External LookupTable Can Manipulate All Price Calculations
description: The `lookupTable` address is set in the constructor and is immutable, but if the LUT contract is upgradeable or has any admin function, a compromised or malicious LUT can return arbitrary `PriceData` (including fabricated high/low prices, precision=0, etc.) to manipulate all reserve calculations. There is no validation on the returned LUT data (e.g., no check that lowPrice < highPrice, precision != 0, or that ratios are within bounds). Specifically: if `pd.lutData.highPrice == pd.lutData.lowPrice`, the `updateReserve` function divides by zero.
message: A malicious or compromised LUT contract can cause division by zero in `updateReserve` (via `highPrice - lowPrice = 0`), return precision=0 causing division by zero in scaledReserves calculations, or manipulate prices to enable profitable sandwich attacks.
exploit_scenario: 1. LUT returns highPrice = lowPrice (e.g., both = 1e6). 2. calcReserveAtRatioSwap calls updateReserve. 3. Division by (pd.lutData.highPrice - pd.lutData.lowPrice) = 0 reverts. OR: LUT returns precision=0, causing division by zero in scaledReserves[j] = scaledReserves[i] * pd.lutData.lowPriceJ / pd.lutData.precision.

title: calcLpTokenSupply Returns 0 Instead of Reverting When Loop Does Not Converge
description: If the Newton's method loop in `calcLpTokenSupply` does not converge within 255 iterations (which can happen with pathological inputs), the function silently returns whatever the last value of `lpTokenSupply` was, rather than reverting. This is inconsistent with `calcReserve` which explicitly reverts. An incorrect lpTokenSupply value used downstream (e.g., in `calcRate` which uses it as `lpTokenSupply`) will corrupt all price calculations.
message: Silently incorrect LP token supply causes wrong prices in calcRate, wrong reserve calculations in calcReserve, and potentially exploitable mispricings in swap functions.
recommendation:
Add a revert after the loop:

revert("calcLpTokenSupply: did not converge");
exploit_scenario: 1. Provide reserves with extreme values that prevent convergence. 2. calcLpTokenSupply returns incorrect non-zero value. 3. calcRate uses this wrong lpTokenSupply to compute prices. 4. Prices are wrong, enabling profitable arbitrage at the expense of LPs.
